summary.text: Prime-by-prime valuation estimates—using Fermat’s theorem and lifting the exponent for odd primes, and an exact calculation when \(n\) is a power of \(2\)—show that every composite \(n\) would have a prime divisor dividing both the quotient defining the relevant term and \(2^{n-2}\), a contradiction. Once \(n\) is prime, any order \(0<q<n-1\) of \(2\) would make \(n\mid 2^q-1\), hence (by cancellation of the factorial denominator) divide the sequence term as well, again contradicting the hypothesis; Fermat’s theorem then gives order exactly \(n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(r)=\frac{2^{r-1}}{r!}\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}(2^j-1)\qquad(r\geq 1).
\]
We prove that if \(n>2\) and
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
then \(n\) is prime and \(2\) has multiplicative order \(n-1\) modulo \(n\).

We first establish the divisibility and valuation estimates needed in the proof. For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\).

### 1. An odd-prime valuation estimate

We will use two standard facts. First, Legendre’s formula says
\[
 v_p(t!)=\sum_{j\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^j}\right\rfloor.       \tag{2}
\]
Second, if \(p\) is odd, Fermat’s theorem gives
\(p\mid 2^{p-1}-1\), and the lifting-the-exponent formula gives, for every positive integer \(r\),
\[
 v_p\bigl(2^{r(p-1)}-1\bigr)
 =v_p\bigl((2^{p-1})^r-1\bigr)
 =v_p(2^{p-1}-1)+v_p(r)
 \geq 1+v_p(r).                                             \tag{3}
\]

For an integer \(m\geq 1\), put
\[
 P_m=\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(2^j-1).
\]
We claim that for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
 v_p(m!)\leq v_p(P_m).                                      \tag{4}
\]

Set
\[
 M=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
For every \(j\geq1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac m{p^j}\right\rfloor
 \leq
 \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p^{j-1}(p-1)}\right\rfloor.         \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, let \(t=\lfloor m/p^j\rfloor\). If \(t=0\), there is nothing to prove. If \(t\geq1\), then
\[
 t p^j\leq m
\]
and hence
\[
 t p^{j-1}(p-1)=t p^j-tp^{j-1}\leq m-1,
\]
because \(tp^{j-1}\geq1\). This proves (5).

Summing (5), using Legendre’s formula and the elementary identity
\[
 \left\lfloor
 \frac{m-1}{p^i(p-1)}
 \right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
we get
\[
 v_p(m!)
 \leq M+\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac M{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =M+v_p(M!).                                                \tag{6}
\]

For each \(1\leq r\leq M\), the index \(r(p-1)\) lies between \(1\) and \(m-1\). Thus all the factors
\(2^{r(p-1)}-1\) occur in \(P_m\). By (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(P_m)
 &\geq \sum_{r=1}^M v_p\bigl(2^{r(p-1)}-1\bigr)\\
 &\geq \sum_{r=1}^M(1+v_p(r))\\
 &=M+v_p(M!).
\end{aligned}
\]
Together with (6), this proves (4).

We also need a strict version. Suppose that
\[
 m=cp-1,\qquad c\geq2,                                     \tag{7}
\]
where \(p\) is an odd prime. Then
\[
 v_p(m!)+1\leq v_p(P_m).                                   \tag{8}
\]
To see this, Legendre’s formula gives the exact identity
\[
 v_p((cp-1)!)=c-1+v_p((c-1)!).                             \tag{9}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{cp-1}{p}\right\rfloor=c-1,
\]
and, for \(j\geq2\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{cp-1}{p^j}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{c-1}{p^{j-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
(The latter follows by first dividing \(cp-1\) by \(p\), whose quotient is \(c-1\), and then by \(p^{j-1}\).)

For every \(1\leq r\leq c\), we have
\[
 r(p-1)\leq c(p-1)=cp-c\leq cp-2=m-1,
\]
where the last inequality uses \(c\geq2\). Hence all \(c\) factors with indices \(r(p-1)\) occur in \(P_m\). Applying (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(P_m)
 &\geq\sum_{r=1}^c(1+v_p(r))\\
 &=c+v_p(c!)\\
 &=c+v_p((c-1)!)+v_p(c)\\
 &\geq c+v_p((c-1)!).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (9), the last quantity is at least \(v_p(m!)+1\), proving (8).

### 2. Integrality of the sequence term

For \(m\geq1\), define
\[
 N_m=2^{m-1}P_m
 =2^{m-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(2^j-1),
 \qquad D_m=m!.
\]
We claim
\[
 D_m\mid N_m.                                               \tag{10}
\]
It is enough to compare valuations at every prime.

For an odd prime \(p\), (4) gives
\[
 v_p(D_m)=v_p(m!)\leq v_p(P_m)\leq v_p(N_m).
\]
For \(p=2\), every factor \(2^j-1\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(N_m)=m-1.
\]
On the other hand, Legendre’s formula gives
\[
 v_2(m!)=\sum_{j\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac m{2^j}\right\rfloor
 \leq m-1
\]
for every \(m\geq1\). Thus the valuation at \(2\) is also sufficient. This proves (10).

Consequently
\[
 a(m)=\frac{N_m}{D_m}                                      \tag{11}
\]
is an integer, in agreement with the displayed formula defining the sequence.

From now on fix \(n>2\) satisfying (1), and put
\[
 m=n-1,\qquad N=N_m,
 \qquad D=D_m,
 \qquad A=\frac ND=a(n-1).
\]
Thus \(D\mid N\), and the hypothesis is
\[
 n\mid A+2^{n-2}.                                          \tag{12}
\]

### 3. Excluding powers of two

We first prove that \(n\) cannot be a power of \(2\). Suppose
\[
 n=2^k.
\]
Since \(n>2\), we have \(k\geq2\). Here \(m=2^k-1\). Since \(P_m\) is odd,
\[
 v_2(N)=m-1=2^k-2.                                         \tag{13}
\]
Legendre’s formula gives the exact value
\[
 v_2((2^k-1)!)=2^k-1-k.                                   \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, for \(1\leq j\leq k\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{2^k-1}{2^j}\right\rfloor=2^{k-j}-1,
\]
and the later terms vanish; hence the sum is
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^k(2^{k-j}-1)=(2^k-1)-k.
\]
Because \(D\mid N\), valuations subtract in the quotient. From (13) and (14),
\[
 v_2(A)=v_2(N)-v_2(D)=k-1.                                 \tag{15}
\]

Also,
\[
 n-2=2^k-2\geq k
\]
for \(k\geq2\), so
\[
 2^k\mid 2^{n-2}.                                          \tag{16}
\]
If (12) held, then \(2^k=n\) would divide \(A+2^{n-2}\). In view of (16), it would then divide \(A\), contradicting (15), which says that only \(2^{k-1}\), not \(2^k\), divides \(A\). Therefore
\[
 n\text{ is not a power of }2.                             \tag{17}
\]

### 4. Excluding every other composite integer

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(n\) is composite. By (17), after removing the highest power of \(2\) from \(n\), an odd factor greater than \(1\) remains. Choose an odd prime divisor \(p\) of that factor. Then
\[
 n=cp
\]
for some positive integer \(c\). Since \(n\) is composite while \(p\) is prime, \(c\neq1\), and therefore
\[
 c\geq2.                                                   \tag{18}
\]
Now
\[
 m=n-1=cp-1.
\]
The strict estimate (8) gives
\[
 v_p(P_m)\geq v_p(m!)+1.                                   \tag{19}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(p\nmid 2^{m-1}\), and hence
\[
 v_p(N)=v_p(P_m).
\]
Using \(D=m!\), (19), and \(D\mid N\), we obtain
\[
 v_p(A)=v_p(N/D)=v_p(N)-v_p(D)\geq1.
\]
Thus
\[
 p\mid A.                                                   \tag{20}
\]
But \(p\mid n\), so (12) also implies
\[
 p\mid A+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting (20), we find
\[
 p\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must equal \(2\), contradicting that \(p\) is odd. This contradiction proves that \(n\) is prime.

### 5. The order of \(2\) modulo \(n\)

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo this prime \(n\). Since \(n>2\), \(n\) is an odd prime, so \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\). Fermat’s theorem gives
\[
 2^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n.                                   \tag{21}
\]
Thus the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) divides \(n-1\). We show that no positive exponent smaller than \(n-1\) can give \(1\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that for some integer \(q\) with
\[
 1\leq q<n-1                                                \tag{22}
\]
we had
\[
 2^q\equiv1\pmod n.
\]
Then
\[
 n\mid 2^q-1.                                               \tag{23}
\]
Because \(q\) lies in the index range \(1,\ldots,m-1=n-2\), the number \(2^q-1\) is one of the factors of
\[
 P_m=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1).
\]
Therefore (23) implies
\[
 n\mid N.                                                   \tag{24}
\]

Since \(n\) is prime and every prime divisor of \((n-1)!\) is at most \(n-1\), we have
\[
 \gcd(n,D)=\gcd(n,(n-1)!)=1.                               \tag{25}
\]
We also know \(N=AD\). Combining (24) and (25), Euclid’s lemma gives
\[
 n\mid A.                                                   \tag{26}
\]
Finally, (12) and (26) imply
\[
 n\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, this would force \(n\mid2\), and hence \(n=2\), contrary to \(n>2\). Thus no \(q\) satisfying (22) can have \(2^q\equiv1\pmod n\).

Together with (21), this proves that the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) is exactly \(n-1\). Since \(n\) is prime, \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Therefore \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), completing the proof.
